claims.statement: Corpus-informed word lists are useful tools for identifying potentially valuable lexical content, but list development and pedagogical use remain purpose-, corpus-, modality- and population-dependent; a published list should be treated as evidence for selection rather than a ready-made curriculum.
claims.limitations: The strongest review evidence concerns vocabulary lists; the same principle must be extended cautiously to constructions and pragmatic routines.

claims.statement: A relatively stable core of high-frequency general English vocabulary exists across large corpora, supporting a portable lexical core for beginners, but the core does not specify the exact order, productive priority or target-task sufficiency of its items.
claims.limitations: General-corpus stability depends on corpus design and lexical counting unit, and a general core underrepresents domain-specific and pragmatic needs.

claims.statement: Raw token frequency alone can misrepresent usefulness because equally frequent items can be distributed very differently across texts/registers; range and dispersion should therefore accompany frequency in corpus-based priority decisions.
claims.limitations: No single dispersion statistic is universally optimal and the desired distribution depends on the target domain.

claims.statement: Corpus-derived content can only generalize to the extent that the corpus represents the target discourse domain; larger corpora are not automatically more relevant, and replication/held-out target corpora can test list generalizability.
claims.limitations: Corpus representativeness is an argument relative to a defined target domain rather than a once-for-all property.

claims.statement: The lexical counting unit materially changes vocabulary-size and coverage estimates; assuming that knowledge of a base word entails knowledge of all derivational family members can overestimate beginner lexical knowledge, especially in Asian EFL contexts.
claims.limitations: Flemma/lemma/family usefulness varies by research/pedagogical purpose; there is no single unit that solves all lexical modeling problems.

claims.statement: A corpus-informed essential beginner list can provide a rational lexical starting pool, but practicability and coverage criteria do not by themselves establish a psycholinguistically optimal teaching sequence.
claims.limitations: The beginner-list work is a selection methodology, not a randomized comparison of alternative teaching orders.

claims.statement: Different defensible high-frequency lists can contain meaningfully different items; in one direct comparison, experienced teachers rated BNC/COCA2000-only items as more useful and 135 Vietnamese EFL learners knew them better than New-GSL-only items, showing that corpus rank should be checked against learner/population evidence.
claims.limitations: The Vietnamese learners were university students mostly above true beginner level; this does not identify near-A0 ordering.

claims.statement: Reading comprehension generally improves continuously as lexical coverage rises; evidence often supports roughly 95% as a minimum useful region and about 98% as a stronger independent-reading region, but these values are not deterministic mastery thresholds.
claims.limitations: Studies differ in learner proficiency, texts, comprehension criteria and counting units; 98% known words does not guarantee comprehension.

claims.statement: Lexical coverage requirements differ by modality: L2 listening can sometimes achieve adequate comprehension below the coverage commonly recommended for reading, with substantial learner variability, so one global vocabulary-size gate across reading/listening/video is invalid.
claims.limitations: The listening study used informal narrative passages and its thresholds should not be generalized to all accents, speeds, tasks or genres.

claims.statement: Lexical coverage is a compatibility indicator between learner and input, not a sufficient explanation of comprehension; discourse processing, background knowledge, syntax, speech processing and task demands still affect performance even at high coverage.
claims.limitations: RQ-027 focuses content selection and does not model every nonlexical source of comprehension difficulty.

claims.statement: Spoken and written registers have meaningfully different lexical distributions, so content intended for conversation/listening should be informed by representative spoken corpora rather than written-frequency lists alone.
claims.limitations: A spoken academic list is not the same target domain as everyday/workplace conversation; modality must be crossed with target needs.

claims.statement: Multiword units and collocations deserve first-class status in content selection because frequent spoken collocations can rival high-frequency single words in occurrence and formulaic multiword sequences show a reliable processing advantage over novel combinations.
claims.limitations: Processing advantage does not imply every frequent sequence should receive deliberate productive instruction.

claims.statement: Frequent nontransparent phrasal expressions create learning demands that single-word lists miss, but receptive usefulness and productive priority must be distinguished when selecting such expressions.
claims.limitations: The PHRASE list was designed especially for receptive use and is corpus/method dependent.

claims.statement: Collocational knowledge is not guaranteed by knowing the component words, and L1 congruency, frequency and exposure affect L2 collocation knowledge; a content model should therefore represent useful combinations separately from their component lexemes.
claims.limitations: Direct Vietnamese evidence is stronger for intermediate/university learners than near-A0 adults.

claims.statement: Usage-based construction evidence supports selecting meaningful form–function patterns with frequent/prototypical exemplars and exemplar diversity rather than treating grammar as a checklist of abstract forms detached from usage.
claims.limitations: Construction-learning evidence does not yield a universal construction syllabus or exact beginner sequence.

claims.statement: High token frequency is not the only useful construction statistic: type frequency, distribution of exemplars, semantic prototypicality, contingency and function can influence learning and productivity.
claims.limitations: Evidence varies by construction family and learner context; weights among these properties remain unresolved.

claims.statement: Pragmatic routines and interaction-organizing expressions should be selected from authentic target discourse because textbooks/self-study materials can underrepresent common functions such as stance, hedging, vague language, clarification and conversational management.
claims.limitations: Corpus frequency alone cannot determine pragmatic appropriateness; context, interlocutor, register and communicative consequence remain essential.

claims.statement: English-as-a-lingua-franca interaction data can reveal portable interactional language absent from native-speaker-oriented textbook models, but no single ELF corpus represents every Vietnamese learner’s future interlocutors or domains.
claims.limitations: ELF is highly heterogeneous; target-needs data from RQ-023 must define which interaction domains matter.

claims.statement: Frequency, perceived usefulness and learning difficulty are related but nonidentical dimensions; combining them can produce different and potentially more defensible teaching priorities than frequency alone.
claims.limitations: Teacher-rated usefulness/difficulty can contain judgment bias and should be triangulated with corpus, learner and target-task evidence.

claims.statement: Target-task language can override general frequency when an item is necessary or high-value for a learner’s real communicative goals; specialized/domain content should therefore branch from a portable core rather than wait for global frequency rank.
claims.limitations: Exact target-task priorities depend on completing direct needs analysis and representative target-discourse collection.

claims.statement: A content item’s learning cost for Vietnamese learners should be informed by observed L1/L2 difficulty and individual evidence rather than stereotypes; population findings on collocation, morphology, pronunciation or grammar function as priors that can increase diagnostic/teaching priority but cannot prove an individual gap.
claims.limitations: Vietnamese-specific studies cover selected constructs and mostly educated learners; direct near-A0 cost estimates remain sparse.

claims.statement: An item with high generative or prerequisite value can deserve early attention when it unlocks many useful exemplars, constructions or target tasks, but generativity must be tied to actual form–meaning/function reuse rather than assumed from grammatical taxonomy.
claims.limitations: No validated universal generativity score exists for beginner English; this is a synthesis criterion requiring curriculum validation.

claims.statement: The content inventory should contain multiple pedagogical unit types—lexemes, multiword units, constructions/form–function patterns and pragmatic routines—because reducing all English content to either single words or grammar rules systematically omits recurrent usage knowledge.
claims.limitations: Unit boundaries can overlap and must not imply mutually exclusive mental representations.

claims.statement: A defensible beginner content selector should combine target-need value, portable general utility, corpus frequency plus range/dispersion, modality/register fit, phrase/construction evidence, coverage contribution, learner-specific gap/cost and generative value rather than optimize any one dimension globally.
claims.limitations: This is the RQ-027 integrative selection model; exact weighting and dominance rules are product/curriculum hypotheses for EXP-027.

claims.statement: Content selection and teaching order are distinct decisions: corpus/needs evidence can determine what deserves inclusion while sequencing must additionally consider learner evidence, prerequisites, processing demands, task progression, recycling and opportunity for later transfer.
claims.limitations: Sequencing interactions are not fully resolved by RQ-027 and must be revisited when RQ-017 is resynthesized after P12.

claims.statement: The exact weights, thresholds and interaction rules among frequency, dispersion, target-task value, formulaicity, modality, coverage, learnability, Vietnamese-L1 cost and generative value remain unresolved for near-A0 adults and require direct held-out corpus and learner validation.
claims.limitations: Explicit validation problem for EXP-027 and later curriculum studies.
